v.q: What is the main difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
o: Symmetric uses one shared key; asymmetric uses a key pair
Symmetric encryption is always slower than asymmetric
Asymmetric encryption works without any keys at all
Symmetric keys can encrypt data but never decrypt it
v.w: Symmetric (AES) is fast and used for bulk data. Asymmetric (RSA, ECC) solves key exchange and signatures but is slower.

v.q: Which statement about symmetric and asymmetric encryption is NOT true?
o: Asymmetric encryption is faster for bulk data
AES is a symmetric cipher
RSA uses a public and private key
Symmetric key sharing is the hard part
v.w: Asymmetric operations are much slower, so bulk data uses a symmetric key that was agreed with asymmetric crypto.

v.q: How does HTTPS (TLS) typically combine the two?
o: Asymmetric crypto agrees a session key, then AES protects the data
TLS uses only RSA to encrypt every byte of the traffic
TLS uses AES with a key that is hard-coded in the browser
TLS hashes all traffic so that nobody can read the content
v.w: The handshake authenticates the server and derives a shared session key. The bulk traffic then uses a symmetric cipher.

v.q: In a TLS connection, what protects the bytes of a large download?
o: A symmetric session key
The server private key directly
A hash of the page
The certificate itself
v.w: The handshake derives a shared session key and a symmetric cipher such as AES-GCM encrypts the traffic.

v.q: Which is the right tool to check that a downloaded file was not tampered with, when you have a trusted published value?
o: A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256
Symmetric encryption with a shared key
Base64 encoding of the downloaded file
Compression of the file before download
v.w: A hash gives a fixed fingerprint. Any change to the input changes it. Base64 is only an encoding, not security.

v.q: Which statement about hash functions is NOT true?
o: A hash can be reversed to get the input back
A small input change changes the output a lot
The output has a fixed length
SHA-256 can check file integrity
v.w: Hashing is one-way. Reversing requires guessing inputs.

v.q: A digital signature is created with which key, and verified with which?
o: Signed with the sender's private key, checked with the public key
Signed with the public key, checked with the private key
Signed and checked with one shared secret value
Signed with the receiver's private key and public key
v.w: Only the owner holds the private key, so a valid signature proves origin and integrity. Anyone can verify with the public key.

v.q: A bank receives a signed payment instruction. What does a valid signature prove?
o: Origin and integrity, not secrecy
The message was kept secret
The recipient has the money
The message was compressed
v.w: A signature gives origin and integrity, not confidentiality. Encrypt the message too if it must stay secret.

v.q: What is a salt in password hashing?
o: A random per-password value mixed in before hashing
A secret key shared by every user of the system
A second hash applied on top of the first hash
An encryption key kept in the user's browser
v.w: Salts are not secret. They make identical passwords hash differently and break precomputed rainbow tables.

v.q: Which statement about salts is NOT true?
o: A salt must be kept secret like a key
A salt is stored with the hash
A salt is random for each password
A salt breaks precomputed rainbow tables
v.w: Salts are not secret. Their job is to make identical passwords hash differently.

v.q: Why must a nonce or IV never be reused with the same key in AES-GCM?
o: Reuse can leak message relationships and break authentication
Reuse makes the encryption noticeably slower for large files
Reuse makes the nonce grow larger than the size of the key
Reuse makes the cipher refuse to start until it is restarted
v.w: GCM nonce reuse is catastrophic: an attacker can recover the authentication key and forge messages. Use a fresh random or counter nonce each time.

v.q: Which practice is correct for AES-GCM?
o: Use a fresh unique nonce for every message
Reuse one nonce to save storage
Derive the nonce from the key
Hard-code the nonce in the source
v.w: A repeated nonce under the same key can reveal plaintext relations and allow forgery, so every message needs a new one.

v.q: What does a certificate authority (CA) provide in public-key infrastructure?
o: A signed statement binding a public key to an identity
The private key belonging to each website
A mechanism that makes the TLS handshake faster
A free allowance of bandwidth for secure sites
v.w: Browsers trust a set of root CAs. A server certificate chains up to one of them, so clients know the key belongs to that domain.

v.q: A browser shows a certificate warning. What did the browser fail to verify?
o: A signature chain to a trusted root CA
The speed of the connection
The size of the page
The language of the site
v.w: A certificate is trusted only when it chains to a root CA in the trust store and matches the domain.

v.q: Which statement about hashing versus encryption is true?
o: Hashing is one-way, encryption can be reversed with the key
Both hashing and encryption can be reversed freely
Hashing can be reversed only with a secret key
Encryption is one-way and cannot be reversed
v.w: Use hashing for passwords and integrity. Use encryption when you must recover the original data.

v.q: Which statement about storing a customer card number is correct?
o: Encrypt it, because you need it back
Hash it, because you need it back
Base64 encode it for protection
Store it as plain text in a protected network
v.w: You must recover the number, so encryption is the tool. Hashing cannot be reversed and Base64 is not security.
